vietnamSoftwareOutsourcing.title: Vietnam Software Outsourcing
vietnamSoftwareOutsourcing.metaTitle: Vietnam Software Outsourcing: Rates, Time Zones & How to Start
vietnamSoftwareOutsourcing.metaDescription: How software outsourcing to Vietnam works for US and European companies — engagement models, time-zone overlap, IP protection, and how Vietnam compares with India, the Philippines, and Poland.
vietnamSoftwareOutsourcing.lede: Software outsourcing to Vietnam means contracting engineering work to a team based in Vietnam, either as a full project team or as engineers embedded in your own. For US and European companies it is most often chosen for the combination of lower engineering cost, a large and growing developer talent pool, and a time zone that gives real overlap with European mornings and US evenings. SofinWave is a Vietnam-based software outsourcing company that works in English and Vietnamese, from architecture through delivery and operations.

sections.heading: What outsourcing to Vietnam actually gets you
sections.body: The reason to outsource is rarely just cost. It is capacity you can add or remove without a hiring cycle, and access to skills you do not want to keep on permanent staff. Vietnam is attractive for that because the engineering market is deep in exactly the stacks most product companies run on.
bullets: Lower blended engineering cost than hiring equivalent seniority in the US, UK, or Western Europe.
A large pool of engineers working in JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Python, Go, and mobile.
English-language delivery: written specs, code review, and demos in English by default.
Capacity that scales up and down on contract terms rather than employment law.

sections.heading: Time zones: what overlap you really get
sections.body: Vietnam is UTC+7 year-round — it does not observe daylight saving, so the offset never shifts. That gives a predictable working relationship with both Europe and the Americas, though the shape of it differs.
bullets: Central Europe (UTC+1/+2): Vietnam is 5–6 hours ahead. A Vietnamese afternoon is a European morning, giving roughly half a working day of live overlap.
UK (UTC+0/+1): 6–7 hours ahead, with a comparable morning overlap window.
US Eastern (UTC-5/-4): 11–12 hours ahead. Overlap sits at the edges — early US morning is late Vietnamese evening — so this pairing works best with a deliberate handoff rhythm.
US Pacific (UTC-8/-7): 14–15 hours ahead, effectively a follow-the-sun model.

sections.heading: How Vietnam compares with other destinations
sections.body: No destination wins on every axis. The honest comparison is about which trade-off suits your team's working style, not which country is objectively best.

sections.heading: Protecting your IP and your code
sections.body: This is the question that stops most outsourcing conversations, and it should be settled in the contract rather than assumed. Vietnam is a signatory to the Berne Convention and the WIPO Copyright Treaty, and standard work-for-hire assignment is enforceable in commercial contracts.
bullets: You own all source code, documentation, and IP produced under the engagement.
NDAs are signed before any technical discovery begins.
Access follows least privilege — engineers get the systems they need and nothing else.
Code lives in your repositories and your cloud accounts, not ours, unless you ask otherwise.

sections.heading: How to start without betting the project on it
sections.body: The lowest-risk way into an outsourcing relationship is a scoped piece of work with a real deliverable, not a trial period with vague goals. You learn more about a team from one shipped increment than from three months of interviews.
bullets: Start with a discovery call to map goals, constraints, and success criteria.
Agree a first slice of work small enough to finish in weeks, not quarters.
Review the code, the tests, and the communication — those tell you what scaling up will feel like.
Expand, adjust the team shape, or stop, with terms agreed up front.

faq.question: Is outsourcing to Vietnam cheaper than hiring locally?
faq.answer: Per engineer, generally yes compared with the US, UK, and Western Europe — but the saving is smaller than headline rate cards suggest once you account for onboarding, overlap hours, and management time. The clearer benefit is that you can add or remove capacity on contract terms rather than through a hiring and redundancy cycle. Ask us for current rates for the roles you need.

faq.question: Will there be a language barrier?
faq.answer: Delivery runs in English by default — specifications, code review, commit messages, demos, and documentation. SofinWave also works in Vietnamese for clients who prefer it. If your team includes non-English speakers, say so early and we will structure written communication accordingly.

faq.question: Who owns the code we pay for?
faq.answer: You do — all source code, documentation, and intellectual property produced under the engagement transfers to you. This is written into the contract before work starts, and we sign an NDA before technical discovery.

faq.question: How quickly can a team start?
faq.answer: It depends on the roles and seniority you need. Tell us the shape of the team and we will give you an honest start date rather than an optimistic one — a team that starts two weeks later but is right costs far less than one that starts immediately and churns.

faq.question: What happens if it does not work out?
faq.answer: Exit terms are agreed at the start, including notice period, handover, and documentation. We hand off cleanly — the point of a good engagement is that your team can pick up the work without us.

cta.title: Talk through whether Vietnam fits your situation
cta.body: A short call is usually enough to tell whether outsourcing helps you or just adds coordination overhead. We will say so either way.

services.title: Services
services.metaDescription: Offshore development, dedicated teams, IT staff augmentation, custom software, system integration, and DevOps — delivered from Vietnam for US and European clients.
services.lede: SofinWave offers six ways to work together, from a full offshore team that owns delivery end to end, to individual engineers embedded in your existing team. Which one fits depends on whether you need capacity, specific skills, or someone to own an outcome. If you are not sure, describe the problem and we will tell you which model we would propose and why.

sections.heading: Team models
sections.body: These three differ in who owns the outcome. Pick by how much of the delivery responsibility you want to keep.
bullets: Offshore development — a complete team that owns delivery of a product or system, with its own process and reporting.
Dedicated team — engineers assigned to you long-term who work inside your process, your board, your standups.
IT staff augmentation — named individuals filling specific gaps in an existing team, managed by you.

sections.heading: Engineering services
sections.body: These are scoped around a technical outcome rather than a team shape, and are usually delivered by one of the models above.
bullets: Custom software development — web, mobile, and backend systems built to your business rules.
System integration — connecting ERP, CRM, payment, and third-party systems into one reliable flow.
DevOps & cloud — CI/CD, infrastructure as code, observability, and cloud cost work.

sections.heading: How to choose
sections.body: The practical test is who will be accountable when a deadline slips. If the answer has to be the vendor, you want offshore development. If your own engineering manager will own it, staff augmentation or a dedicated team is a better fit and usually cheaper.

faq.question: Can we change model partway through?
faq.answer: Yes, and it is common. Engagements often start as a scoped project and move to a dedicated team once the direction is clear. Changing model is a contract amendment, not a restart.

faq.question: Do you take on work on an existing codebase?
faq.answer: Yes. Most of our work is on systems that already exist and already have users. We start with a short read-through of the code and infrastructure before quoting anything.

faq.question: What is the smallest engagement you take?
faq.answer: Small enough to be a real test of whether we work well together. Tell us the first slice you would want delivered and we will say whether it is a sensible starting point.

cta.title: Tell us what you are building
cta.body: Send a short description of the system and the constraint you are hitting. We reply within one business day.

offshoreDevelopment.title: Offshore Software Development
offshoreDevelopment.metaTitle: Offshore Software Development Services in Vietnam
offshoreDevelopment.metaDescription: A complete offshore development team in Vietnam that owns delivery end to end — architecture, build, testing, release, and operations — for US and European companies.
offshoreDevelopment.lede: Offshore software development means a vendor team, in another country, that owns delivery of a product or system rather than just supplying hands. SofinWave runs offshore teams from Vietnam for US and European clients: we take a defined outcome, staff the roles it needs, and are accountable for shipping it. You get progress you can verify — running software, not status decks.

sections.heading: What the team looks like
sections.body: An offshore team is staffed to the work rather than to a template. A typical product team pairs engineers with the supporting roles that stop delivery from stalling.
bullets: A technical lead accountable for architecture and code quality.
Backend, frontend, and mobile engineers sized to the scope.
QA embedded in the team rather than bolted on at the end.
A delivery lead who runs the cadence and is your single point of contact.

sections.heading: How delivery runs
sections.body: The process is deliberately boring, because predictability is the point. Work moves in short iterations with a demo at the end of each, so you never have to take progress on trust.
bullets: Discovery first: goals, constraints, and success metrics written down before code.
Iterations of one to two weeks, each ending in a demo of working software.
Automated tests and CI from the first commit, not retrofitted before launch.
Releases into your environment through a repeatable pipeline.

sections.heading: What you keep control of
sections.body: Offshoring delivery does not mean giving up oversight. The artefacts that matter stay yours and stay visible throughout.
bullets: Your repositories, your cloud accounts, your CI — we work inside them.
Full commit history and code review visibility from day one.
Architecture decisions written down and approved by you before implementation.
Documentation maintained as part of the work, so handover is not a separate project.

sections.heading: When offshore development is the wrong choice
sections.body: If the requirements change faster than they can be written down, or the work depends on constant access to people inside your business, a vendor team will struggle regardless of quality. In that situation a dedicated team inside your own process, or staff augmentation, usually works better — and we will say so rather than sell you the larger engagement.

faq.question: How is this different from a dedicated team?
faq.answer: Accountability. With offshore development we own the outcome and run our own process. With a dedicated team, your managers run the process and the engineers work inside it. Offshore development costs more per engineer and removes more management load from you.

faq.question: How do we track progress?
faq.answer: Through working software at the end of every iteration, plus direct access to the repository and issue tracker. If a progress report is the only evidence of progress, something has gone wrong.

faq.question: What if we want to bring the work in-house later?
faq.answer: That is a normal outcome, and the engagement is set up for it. Documentation and tests are produced throughout, and handover terms are agreed at the start rather than negotiated under pressure.

faq.question: Do you work fixed-price or time-and-materials?
faq.answer: Both. Fixed-price suits well-defined scope; time-and-materials suits work that will evolve. See engagement models for how we decide which to propose.

dedicatedTeam.title: Dedicated Development Team
dedicatedTeam.metaDescription: Hire a dedicated development team in Vietnam that works inside your process, your tools, and your roadmap — long-term engineers without the hiring cycle.
dedicatedTeam.lede: A dedicated development team is a group of engineers assigned to you long-term who work inside your process rather than a vendor's. They join your standups, pull from your backlog, and are reviewed by your leads. You get the continuity of in-house staff without carrying the hiring cycle, and you can change the team's shape as the roadmap changes.

sections.heading: How it works in practice
sections.body: The team is yours to direct. We handle recruitment, employment, equipment, and retention; you handle what they work on.
bullets: You define the roles and interview the candidates before they join.
Engineers work in your repositories, your tracker, and your ceremonies.
Your engineering manager sets priorities and reviews the work.
We handle contracts, payroll, hardware, and replacement if someone leaves.

sections.heading: Why continuity matters more than headcount
sections.body: The expensive part of any engineering team is context — knowing why the system is shaped the way it is. A dedicated team is worth more in month six than month one, which is why we structure these engagements for retention rather than churn. If an engineer has to be replaced, the handover happens with overlap, not a gap.

sections.heading: Choosing between the three models
sections.body: The distinction that matters is who is accountable when something slips. Use this to decide which conversation to start.

faq.question: Can we interview the engineers?
faq.answer: Yes, and you should. You define the role, we shortlist, you interview and decide. Nobody joins your team without your approval.

faq.question: What is the minimum commitment?
faq.answer: Dedicated teams only make economic sense over a longer horizon, because the ramp-up is paid once and returned over time. For short or uncertain needs, staff augmentation is the cheaper answer.

faq.question: What happens if an engineer leaves?
faq.answer: We replace them and run an overlap so context transfers rather than evaporates. Retention is our cost to bear, not yours.

faq.question: Can the team grow or shrink?
faq.answer: Yes, with notice agreed in the contract. Scaling down is as much a part of the arrangement as scaling up — that flexibility is a large part of why teams outsource at all.

staffAugmentation.title: IT Staff Augmentation
staffAugmentation.metaTitle: IT Staff Augmentation Services from Vietnam
staffAugmentation.metaDescription: Add named senior engineers to your existing team for weeks or months. IT staff augmentation from Vietnam — you manage the work, we handle everything else.
staffAugmentation.lede: IT staff augmentation means adding named individual engineers to your existing team for a defined period. You manage them exactly as you manage your own staff; we handle contracts, payroll, and equipment. It is the fastest and lowest-commitment way to work with us, and the right answer when you know precisely which skill is missing.

sections.heading: When augmentation beats hiring
sections.body: Permanent hiring is the right answer for durable, core capability. Augmentation is better when the need has an end date, or when you cannot afford to wait out a hiring cycle.
bullets: A deadline that needs more hands than you have, for a known period.
A specific skill — a mobile platform, a database, a cloud migration — you need once.
Cover for parental leave, notice periods, or an unexpected departure.
Testing whether a role is genuinely needed before opening a permanent headcount.

sections.heading: What we handle and what you handle
sections.body: The division is deliberately simple, because ambiguity about who manages an engineer is the usual reason augmentation fails.
bullets: You: priorities, code review, day-to-day direction, performance feedback.
Us: sourcing, contracts, payroll, equipment, and replacement if needed.
Both: an agreed check-in so problems surface early rather than at renewal.

sections.heading: The honest limitation
sections.body: Augmented engineers work well when your team already has clear direction and a functioning review process. If the constraint is that nobody has time to direct the work, adding engineers makes it worse, not better. In that case a dedicated team with its own lead, or an offshore team that owns the outcome, is the better structure — say so early and we will propose accordingly.

faq.question: How quickly can someone start?
faq.answer: Faster than a dedicated team, since there is no team-building step, but it still depends on the skill. Rare specialisms take longer to source than common ones. We give you a real date, not a hopeful one.

faq.question: Do we get the same person throughout?
faq.answer: Yes. Augmentation is named individuals, not interchangeable capacity. If a change is unavoidable we tell you early and run an overlap.

faq.question: What is the shortest engagement?
faq.answer: Short engagements are possible but rarely worth it — the first weeks are mostly context-building, so very short contracts spend most of their value on ramp-up. Tell us the deadline you are working to and we will be straight about whether it is worth starting.

customSoftwareDevelopment.title: Custom Software Development
customSoftwareDevelopment.metaDescription: Custom web, mobile, and backend software built around your business rules — designed, built, tested, and operated by a Vietnam-based engineering team.
customSoftwareDevelopment.lede: Custom software development means building a system around your business rules instead of bending your business around a product you bought. It is worth doing when the process you run is the thing that makes you competitive, and worth avoiding when an off-the-shelf tool would do the job. We will tell you which situation you are in before quoting.

sections.heading: What we build
sections.body: Most of our work is line-of-business systems — the software a company runs on rather than the software it sells, though we build products too.
bullets: Web applications and internal platforms, typically TypeScript with React or Next.js.
Backend services and APIs in Node.js, Python, or Go, with PostgreSQL behind them.
Mobile applications where a browser is genuinely not enough.
Data pipelines and reporting where the reporting is the product.

sections.heading: Build versus buy
sections.body: The honest test is whether the process is a differentiator or just a cost. If a competitor could buy the same capability off the shelf and be no worse off, buy it. Build when the rules are specific to how you win, when integration with what you already run is the hard part, or when licence costs at your scale exceed what building would cost.

sections.heading: How we keep it maintainable
sections.body: The expensive part of custom software is not writing it, it is living with it. Everything we build is set up so that another team could take it over.
bullets: Automated tests written alongside features, not retrofitted.
Architecture decisions recorded with their reasoning, so future changes are informed.
Boring, conventional choices unless there is a specific reason not to be.
Deployment automated from the first release, so shipping never depends on one person.

faq.question: How do you estimate a build?
faq.answer: After discovery, not before. An estimate given before anyone has looked at your constraints is a guess with a number attached. Discovery is short and paid, and it produces a plan you can take elsewhere if you want to.

faq.question: Can you work with our existing system?
faq.answer: Yes, and most of our work is exactly that. Greenfield projects are the exception. We start by reading the code and the infrastructure before proposing anything.

faq.question: What technologies do you use?
faq.answer: Mainly TypeScript, Node.js, React and Next.js, Python, Go, PostgreSQL, Kubernetes, and AWS. We pick from what your team can maintain, not from what is newest.

systemIntegration.title: System Integration
systemIntegration.metaTitle: System Integration Services: ERP, CRM & Payments
systemIntegration.metaDescription: Connect ERP, CRM, payment, and third-party systems into one reliable flow. System integration services with an emphasis on failure handling and observability.
systemIntegration.lede: System integration is the work of making separate systems behave as one — moving data between an ERP, a CRM, a payment provider, and whatever else the business runs on, reliably enough that nobody re-keys it by hand. The hard part is almost never the happy path. It is what happens when one system is down, slow, or returns something unexpected.

sections.heading: What integration work usually looks like
sections.body: Most integration projects start because someone is copying data between systems manually, and the cost of that has finally become visible.
bullets: ERP and accounting systems that need order and inventory data from elsewhere.
Payment providers, where correctness and reconciliation matter more than speed.
CRM and marketing tools that need a trustworthy customer record.
Legacy systems with no modern API, reached through files, queues, or a database.

sections.heading: Designing for the unhappy path
sections.body: An integration that only works when every system is healthy is not finished. We design for partial failure from the start, because in production it is the normal condition rather than the exception.
bullets: Idempotent operations, so a retry cannot double-charge or duplicate an order.
Explicit retry and backoff rules rather than hoping the next attempt succeeds.
Dead-letter handling so failed messages are visible instead of silently lost.
Reconciliation checks that catch drift between systems before a customer does.

sections.heading: Making it observable
sections.body: When an integration misbehaves, the first question is always where a record stopped. If answering that means reading logs on four systems, incidents take hours instead of minutes. We instrument the flow end to end so that question has a single answer.

faq.question: Can you integrate a system with no API?
faq.answer: Usually yes. Older systems are commonly reached through scheduled file exchange, database access, or a message queue. It is less elegant but entirely workable, and we will be clear about the trade-offs before committing.

faq.question: How do you handle data that disagrees between systems?
faq.answer: By deciding, explicitly and with you, which system is authoritative for each field before writing any code. Most integration pain comes from that decision being made implicitly.

faq.question: Do you support the integration after it ships?
faq.answer: We can. Integrations break when systems on either end change, so ongoing support is often worth more than the initial build. Alternatively we hand over with documentation and runbooks.

devopsCloud.title: DevOps & Cloud
devopsCloud.metaDescription: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code, observability, Kubernetes, and cloud cost work — DevOps outsourcing from Vietnam for teams that need releases to stop hurting.
devopsCloud.lede: DevOps work is what turns releasing software from an event into a routine. We build the pipelines, infrastructure definitions, and monitoring that let a team deploy on a Tuesday afternoon without anyone holding their breath. It is usually the highest-leverage work available to a team that is shipping slowly, because it compounds across every future release.

sections.heading: Where we usually start
sections.body: The first question is what makes releasing painful today. The answer determines the order of work, and it is rarely the thing people expect.
bullets: CI/CD: automated build, test, and deploy so releases are repeatable.
Infrastructure as code, so environments can be recreated rather than remembered.
Observability: logs, metrics, and traces that answer questions during an incident.
Cloud cost: finding the spend that is not buying anything.

sections.heading: Kubernetes, but only when it earns its place
sections.body: Kubernetes solves real problems at real scale, and creates new ones below that scale. We run it where the workload justifies the operational cost, and recommend something simpler where it does not. A platform your team cannot debug at 3am is a liability regardless of how modern it is.

sections.heading: Cloud migration without a big bang
sections.body: Migrations fail when they are all-or-nothing. We move workloads incrementally, with the ability to roll back at each step, and we measure cost and performance before and after so the business case is verified rather than assumed.

faq.question: Which cloud providers do you work with?
faq.answer: Mostly AWS, and we work with others where that is what you already run. Migrating cloud provider is rarely worth doing on its own — the gains usually come from how workloads are architected, not from whose logo is on the bill.

faq.question: Can you reduce our cloud bill?
faq.answer: Often, yes, and the first pass usually finds idle resources, oversized instances, and storage nobody owns. We report what we find and what it would take to fix, so you can decide what is worth doing.

faq.question: Do you provide on-call support?
faq.answer: We can operate what we build, including monitoring and response. Terms depend on the coverage you need — tell us your availability requirements and we will be concrete about what is realistic.

engagementModels.title: Engagement Models & Pricing
engagementModels.metaTitle: Engagement Models: Fixed Price vs Time and Materials
engagementModels.metaDescription: How SofinWave prices software outsourcing work — fixed price, time and materials, and dedicated capacity — and which one to choose for your project.
engagementModels.lede: There are three ways to pay for software work, and the right one depends entirely on how well the scope is known. Fixed price suits work that can be fully specified in advance. Time and materials suits work that will change as you learn. Dedicated capacity suits ongoing work with no defined end. Choosing wrong is the most common reason outsourcing relationships turn adversarial.

sections.heading: Fixed price
sections.body: You agree a scope, a price, and a date. It works when the requirements genuinely can be pinned down, and it fails badly when they cannot — because every change becomes a negotiation instead of a decision.
bullets: Best for: well-understood scope, a migration, a defined integration, a rebuild of something that already exists.
You get: budget certainty and a clear definition of done.
The trade-off: change costs more, because the price already priced in the risk of it.
Requires: discovery first. We do not quote fixed price on a brief alone.

sections.heading: Time and materials
sections.body: You pay for the effort actually spent, at agreed rates, with a cap and regular review. It is the honest model for anything genuinely new, because it does not force either side to pretend the scope is knowable.
bullets: Best for: new products, evolving requirements, and work where discovery continues as you build.
You get: the ability to change direction without renegotiating a contract.
The trade-off: you carry the scope risk, so forecasting and reporting matter more.
We include: an agreed cap and a regular review point, so it never runs unbounded.

sections.heading: Dedicated capacity
sections.body: You pay monthly for an agreed team, and direct their work yourself. It is the simplest model to reason about, and the most economical over a long horizon because ramp-up is paid once rather than at every project boundary.
bullets: Best for: ongoing product development with no defined end date.
You get: predictable monthly cost and a team that accumulates context.
The trade-off: it only pays off over months, so it is a poor fit for short needs.
Notice periods for scaling down are agreed at the start.

sections.heading: How we actually decide

fintech.title: Fintech Software Development
fintech.metaDescription: Payments, ledgers, reconciliation, and regulated financial systems built by an engineering team that treats correctness and auditability as requirements, not features.
fintech.lede: Fintech software has a property most software does not: being approximately right is the same as being wrong. A ledger that loses a cent, a payment that gets retried into a double charge, or a report that cannot be reconciled are not cosmetic bugs. We build financial systems with correctness, auditability, and failure handling designed in from the first commit rather than added after an incident.

sections.heading: What we build in this space
sections.body: The work concentrates around money movement and the records that prove it happened.
bullets: Payment integrations and the reconciliation that proves they balance.
Double-entry ledgers and transaction records built to be audited.
Onboarding and KYC flows that respect both compliance and completion rates.
Reporting where the numbers have to survive scrutiny.

sections.heading: Correctness as an engineering discipline
sections.body: In financial systems the interesting cases are the ones that happen once in a million transactions, because at volume they happen daily. We design for them explicitly.
bullets: Idempotency on every operation that moves money.
Immutable transaction records — corrections are new entries, never edits.
Reconciliation jobs that detect drift before a customer or auditor does.
Explicit handling of partial failure between systems and providers.

sections.heading: Working with regulated requirements
sections.body: We are engineers, not your compliance advisers, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we do is build systems that make compliance demonstrable — access controls, audit trails, data retention, and evidence that can be produced on request. Your legal and compliance function defines the obligation; we make sure the software can prove it was met.

faq.question: Have you worked on regulated financial systems?
faq.answer: Our team has delivered production systems handling payments and financial records. For specifics relevant to your situation, ask on a call — we would rather discuss real detail under NDA than publish vague claims.

faq.question: Can you work with our existing payment provider?
faq.answer: Yes. Most fintech work is integration with providers already chosen. We start by reading their API semantics carefully, particularly around retries, webhooks, and settlement timing, since that is where most defects originate.

faq.question: How do you handle sensitive financial data?
faq.answer: Least-privilege access, data minimisation, encryption in transit and at rest, and no production data in development environments. Specific controls are agreed with you before work starts.

ecommerce.title: E-commerce Development
ecommerce.metaDescription: Storefronts, checkout, inventory, and order systems engineered for peak traffic — e-commerce development outsourcing for teams whose revenue depends on uptime.
ecommerce.lede: E-commerce engineering is judged on two days a year. A platform that is fast in March and falls over on Black Friday has failed, regardless of how well it performs on average. We build and re-architect commerce systems for the peak rather than the mean, and for the parts customers notice most: checkout, search, and whether the stock number is true.

sections.heading: Where commerce systems usually hurt
sections.body: The failure modes repeat across businesses, and they are rarely in the storefront itself.
bullets: Checkout that degrades under load, precisely when it is most expensive to lose.
Inventory that drifts from reality, causing oversells and manual reconciliation.
Order flows tangled across a shop platform, an ERP, and a warehouse system.
Search and catalogue performance that quietly suppresses conversion.

sections.heading: Engineering for peak, not average
sections.body: Capacity planning based on average traffic guarantees a bad peak. We load-test against realistic peak profiles, find where the system actually breaks, and fix that rather than the part that looked risky.
bullets: Load testing against realistic traffic shapes before the season, not after.
Caching strategies that stay correct when prices and stock change.
Graceful degradation, so a failing recommendation service never blocks a purchase.
Observability tight enough to diagnose during a peak rather than afterwards.

sections.heading: Replatforming without losing a season
sections.body: Full rewrites of commerce systems are risky because the deadline is set by the calendar, not by you. We prefer incremental replacement — moving one capability at a time behind a stable interface — so that at every point there is a working system and a way back.

faq.question: Do you work with existing commerce platforms?
faq.answer: Yes. Much of the work is extending or integrating platforms already in place rather than replacing them, and replacement is usually the more expensive answer to the wrong question.

faq.question: Can you help before a peak season?
faq.answer: Yes, and the earlier the better. Load testing and remediation take time; work started weeks before a peak is far more useful than work started days before.

faq.question: How do you handle inventory accuracy?
faq.answer: By deciding explicitly which system is authoritative for stock, then designing the flow so every other system reconciles against it. Most oversell problems are ownership problems rather than technical ones.

logistics.title: Logistics Software Development
logistics.metaDescription: Warehouse, transport, and tracking systems that stay correct when the network does not — logistics software development for operations that run in the physical world.
logistics.lede: Logistics software models a physical world that does not cooperate. Scanners lose connectivity, drivers go through tunnels, and a parcel exists whether or not the system knows where it is. Systems that assume reliable connectivity and tidy data fail in exactly the conditions they were built for. We design logistics systems around intermittency and correction rather than around the happy path.

sections.heading: What we build
sections.body: The work spans the warehouse floor, the road, and the reporting that ties them together.
bullets: Warehouse and inventory systems, including handheld and offline-capable interfaces.
Transport and route planning, plus driver-facing applications.
Track-and-trace with event histories that survive out-of-order updates.
Integrations with carriers, customs, ERP, and customer portals.

sections.heading: Designing for intermittent connectivity
sections.body: Anything used in a warehouse or a vehicle will lose its connection. That is a design input, not an incident, and treating it as an incident is how these systems accumulate manual workarounds.
bullets: Offline-first data capture that queues and syncs when connectivity returns.
Conflict resolution rules decided in advance rather than improvised.
Event models that tolerate updates arriving late or out of order.
Interfaces usable one-handed, wearing gloves, in poor light.

sections.heading: When the data and the world disagree
sections.body: In logistics they always eventually do. The question is whether the system makes the discrepancy visible and correctable, or hides it until a customer calls. We build in reconciliation and correction paths, with an audit trail, so that fixing reality is a normal operation rather than a database edit.

faq.question: Can you integrate with carrier systems?
faq.answer: Yes. Carrier integrations are a routine part of this work, and their quirks — inconsistent status vocabularies, delayed webhooks, out-of-order events — are exactly what the design has to absorb.

faq.question: Do you build mobile apps for drivers and warehouse staff?
faq.answer: Yes, with offline capability where the environment demands it. Usability under real conditions matters more here than in most software: cold hands, gloves, and bad lighting are design constraints.

faq.question: Can you work with our existing WMS or TMS?
faq.answer: Usually. Replacing a working warehouse or transport system is disruptive and rarely the cheapest route. We more often extend and integrate what is already running.

aiImplementation.title: AI System Implementation
aiImplementation.metaDescription: Take an AI idea from prototype to a production system with evaluation, monitoring, and cost control. AI implementation consulting and engineering from Vietnam.
aiImplementation.lede: AI implementation is the work between a demo that impresses and a system you can put in front of customers. The model is rarely the hard part. The hard parts are evaluation you can trust, latency and cost that survive real traffic, and behaviour that stays acceptable when users do things nobody anticipated. We build AI systems the same way we build any production system: with tests, monitoring, and a rollback path.

sections.heading: Why AI prototypes stall before production
sections.body: Most teams get to a convincing demo quickly and then stop. The reasons are consistent, and none of them are about model choice.
bullets: No evaluation set, so nobody can tell whether a change made things better or worse.
Costs that were trivial in testing become the largest line item at real volume.
Latency that is fine for one user is unacceptable when requests queue.
No plan for the cases where the model is confidently wrong.
Nothing logged, so failures cannot be reproduced or explained to a customer.

sections.heading: What we build first
sections.body: Before adding capability, we make the system measurable. Otherwise every later change is a guess.
bullets: An evaluation set drawn from your real data, with the failure cases included.
Automated scoring in CI, so a prompt or model change is a measurable event.
Tracing on every call: inputs, outputs, latency, tokens, and cost per request.
A guardrail layer for the outputs that must never reach a user unchecked.

sections.heading: Choosing the smallest thing that works
sections.body: Fine-tuning, retrieval, agents, and a bigger model are four different answers to four different problems, and they are routinely applied to the wrong one. Retrieval fixes missing knowledge. Fine-tuning fixes format and tone. Agents fix multi-step workflows. A bigger model fixes reasoning depth, at a cost. We diagnose which you actually have before building, because the expensive option is often solving a problem you do not have.

sections.heading: Keeping it affordable at volume
sections.body: AI cost scales with usage in a way most software does not, and a system that is profitable at a thousand requests a day can be ruinous at a hundred thousand. We design for that from the start.
bullets: Caching for the requests that repeat, which is usually more of them than expected.
Routing cheap requests to small models and reserving large ones for hard cases.
Prompt and context trimming, measured rather than assumed.
Cost dashboards per feature, so an expensive path is visible before the invoice.

sections.heading: When we will tell you not to use AI
sections.body: Plenty of problems presented as AI problems are search problems, rules problems, or data-quality problems, and solving them conventionally is cheaper, faster, and more predictable. If that is what we find, we will say so. A recommendation engine that is a well-tuned query beats one that hallucinates, and it costs a fraction to run.

faq.question: Do we need our own model?
faq.answer: Almost never. Most production systems use a hosted model with retrieval and good prompting. Training or fine-tuning your own is worth it for narrow, high-volume, format-sensitive tasks — and it is a much larger commitment. We will tell you which case you are in before you spend on it.

faq.question: How do you stop it producing wrong answers?
faq.answer: You cannot eliminate it, so the system has to handle it. That means grounding answers in your data with citations, validating structured outputs against a schema, gating high-risk actions behind human confirmation, and logging enough to explain any specific answer afterwards.

faq.question: Can this run on our own infrastructure?
faq.answer: Yes, where the data requires it. Self-hosting open-weight models trades API cost for operational cost and lower ceiling on capability. That trade is worth making for some data-sensitive workloads and not for others — we will be concrete about which.

faq.question: How do you measure whether it is good enough?
faq.answer: Against an evaluation set built from your data with agreed pass criteria, before launch. "It seems better" is not a release criterion, and without a baseline nobody can tell whether the next change helped.

llmIntegration.title: LLM Integration & RAG
llmIntegration.metaTitle: LLM Integration and RAG Development Services
llmIntegration.metaDescription: Connect a language model to your own data and product — retrieval-augmented generation, structured outputs, and evaluation built for production rather than demos.
llmIntegration.lede: LLM integration means connecting a language model to your data and your product so it answers from what you actually know rather than what it was trained on. In practice that is retrieval-augmented generation: find the right context, give it to the model, and cite where the answer came from. Most of the engineering effort goes into retrieval quality, not into the model call.

sections.heading: Retrieval is where RAG succeeds or fails
sections.body: If the right passage is not retrieved, no model can answer correctly. Teams typically discover this after blaming the model for months.
bullets: Chunking that respects document structure rather than cutting at a fixed length.
Hybrid search — keyword alongside vectors, because exact terms still matter.
Reranking the candidate set before it reaches the model's context.
Retrieval measured on its own: was the right passage in the top results at all?

sections.heading: Making outputs safe to use programmatically
sections.body: A model that returns prose is fine for a chat window and useless as an input to the rest of your system. When the output feeds code, it needs to be structured and validated.
bullets: Schema-constrained outputs, validated before anything downstream consumes them.
Explicit handling for the model declining or returning nothing usable.
Citations back to source documents, so a user can check the claim.
Deterministic fallbacks when the confident answer is not good enough to ship.

sections.heading: Keeping the index current
sections.body: A retrieval system quietly decays as the underlying documents change. We build the ingestion pipeline as a first-class part of the system — incremental updates, deletion handling, and a way to tell how stale the index is — because a confidently wrong answer sourced from a deleted document is worse than no answer.

faq.question: What is RAG in plain terms?
faq.answer: Retrieval-augmented generation: before answering, the system searches your documents for relevant passages and includes them in the model's context. The model then answers from that material and cites it, instead of relying on what it memorised during training.

faq.question: Can it answer from our private data without that data training the model?
faq.answer: Yes. Retrieval puts your data into the request, not into the model's weights. Whether the provider retains request data depends on the provider and plan, which is a contract question we can help you check before you commit.

faq.question: Which vector database should we use?
faq.answer: For most workloads, PostgreSQL with pgvector is sufficient and avoids adding a component to operate. Dedicated vector databases start to earn their place at large scale or with demanding filtering. We would rather add one when your numbers justify it.

faq.question: How do we know retrieval is working?
faq.answer: By measuring it separately from generation. We build a set of questions with known correct sources and track whether those sources appear in the retrieved results. That number tells you where to invest — most of the time it is retrieval, not the model.

aiAgents.title: AI Agent Development
aiAgents.metaDescription: Agentic systems that carry out multi-step work against your tools, with permissions, audit trails, and a human in the loop where it matters.
aiAgents.lede: An AI agent is a system that decides which steps to take and calls your tools to take them, rather than producing text for a person to act on. That makes it useful for multi-step work and risky in exactly the same measure — an agent with write access can do real damage quickly. We build agents with narrow permissions, full audit trails, and human confirmation on anything expensive or irreversible.

sections.heading: Where agents genuinely earn their place
sections.body: Agents suit work with a clear goal, several steps, and tolerance for a retry. They suit high-volume, zero-tolerance transaction processing far less.
bullets: Triage and routing: read an incoming item, classify it, act or escalate.
Research and summarisation across several internal systems.
Multi-step back-office work that currently means a person copying between tools.
Drafting that a human reviews and approves before anything is sent.

sections.heading: Permissions and blast radius
sections.body: The design question is not what the agent can do when it works, but what it can do when it is wrong. We answer that before building anything.
bullets: Least-privilege tool access — read-only by default, write granted case by case.
Explicit human confirmation for spending, sending, or deleting.
Rate and budget limits per run, so a loop cannot become an invoice.
A full trace of every step, so any action can be explained afterwards.

sections.heading: Making agents testable
sections.body: An agent that behaves differently every run is not something you can maintain. We pin down what can be pinned: deterministic tools with their own tests, recorded traces replayed as regression cases, and evaluation over whole runs rather than single responses. Without that, every change is a gamble and nobody will trust the system enough to widen its permissions.

faq.question: How is an agent different from a chatbot?
faq.answer: A chatbot produces text for a person to act on. An agent takes the actions itself by calling tools — querying a database, opening a ticket, sending a message. That difference is why permissions and audit trails matter far more than they do for a chat interface.

faq.question: What if the agent does something wrong?
faq.answer: Assume it will, and design so the consequences are bounded. Irreversible and expensive actions sit behind human confirmation, tool access is minimal, and every step is logged in enough detail to reconstruct and reverse what happened.

faq.question: Can it work with our existing tools?
faq.answer: Yes — agents act through whatever APIs you already have. Where a system has no API, the same file, queue, or database routes we use for conventional integration apply.

faq.question: Is this worth doing yet?
faq.answer: For bounded, reviewable work, often yes. For unattended, high-stakes, high-volume processing, usually not yet. We would rather tell you that than build something you have to turn off in a month.

sections.heading: What this site is
sections.body: A working notebook, published. We write things down to think more clearly and to be able to check later whether our reasoning held up.
bullets: How we frame decisions, and the checklists we run before acting.
Post-mortems on our own decisions, including the ones that went badly.
Tools we built for our own analysis, and what they do and do not tell you.
Notes on data sources, and where they mislead.

sections.heading: What this site is not
sections.body: It is not advice, and it is not a signal service. SofinWave is not a licensed investment adviser and does not provide investment advice, portfolio management, or brokerage services. Everything here describes our own process and is published for general information only. We do not manage money for anyone, we do not sell recommendations, and nothing here accounts for your circumstances, obligations, or risk tolerance — none of which we know.

sections.heading: Why an engineering team writes about investing
sections.body: For the same reason we write about anything: we build tools for the problems we have. Most published investing content is either marketing for a product or a signal service with no track record. We would rather show the process, including where it failed, and let you judge it. If that is useful to you, good. If you want advice, speak to someone licensed to give it.

sections.heading: On the tools
sections.body: The tools here are the ones we built for ourselves — screeners, trackers, and analysis scripts. They compute things; they do not decide anything. Any tool that outputs a number invites you to trust the number more than it deserves, and we try to document the assumptions rather than hide them behind an interface.

faq.question: Do you offer investment advice?
faq.answer: No. SofinWave is not a licensed investment adviser and does not provide investment advice, portfolio management, or brokerage services. Everything here describes our own process and is published for general information only. If you want advice tailored to your situation, consult a licensed adviser in your jurisdiction.

faq.question: Do you manage money for clients?

faq.question: Can I copy what you do?
faq.answer: You can read what we do and why. Whether it suits you depends on your circumstances, time horizon, and tolerance for loss — which we know nothing about. Past results, ours included, do not predict future ones.

faq.question: Why publish this at all?
faq.answer: Writing forces clarity, and publishing forces honesty about the decisions that went wrong. The archive is more useful to us than to anyone else; it is public because there is no reason for it not to be.

home.title: SofinWave Academy
home.metaTitle: SofinWave Academy — Engineering, Investing & School Tutoring
home.metaDescription: Courses and tutoring in software engineering and AI, investing literacy, content production, and school subjects for grades 1-12.
home.lede: SofinWave Academy teaches what our team does for a living, plus school tutoring for grades 1 to 12. The engineering material started as our internal onboarding — the documents we wrote to bring new engineers up to speed — and the rest grew from the same habit of writing things down properly. Small groups, working examples, and instructors who still do the work.

sections.heading: What we teach
sections.body: Four areas, taught by people who practise them rather than by career instructors.
bullets: Software engineering: TypeScript, backend systems, architecture, and testing.
AI in practice: building and evaluating LLM applications rather than theory.
Investing literacy: how to read a company and think about risk. Not advice.
Content production: filming, editing, and writing that holds attention.
School subjects, grades 1-12: maths, sciences, and English.

sections.heading: How the classes run
sections.body: Small groups, with real work rather than lectures. Every session ends with something the student has built, solved, or written.
bullets: Small cohorts, so questions get answered when they are asked.
Projects and exercises drawn from problems we have actually faced.
Recorded sessions and written material to review afterwards.
Taught in Vietnamese or English.

sections.heading: On the investing courses
sections.body: These teach how to read financial statements, understand risk, and think about valuation. They are financial education, not investment advice — we are not licensed advisers, we will not tell anyone what to buy, and no course outcome should be read as a promise of returns.

sections.heading: On school tutoring
sections.body: For grades 1 to 12 we teach maths, sciences, and English, and we are honest about the scope: this is small-group tutoring built around understanding rather than a full curriculum replacement, and it works best alongside school rather than instead of it.

faq.question: Who teaches the courses?
faq.answer: Practising engineers and consultants from SofinWave. The people teaching the engineering material are the same people writing production code that week.

faq.question: What languages are classes in?
faq.answer: Vietnamese or English, depending on the cohort. Written material is generally provided in both.

faq.question: Do the investing courses tell me what to buy?
faq.answer: No. They teach how to analyse and how to think about risk. We are not licensed to give investment advice and will not do so in a classroom either.

faq.question: Do you teach beginners?
faq.answer: Yes, for most subjects. Where a course assumes prior knowledge, the prerequisites are stated up front rather than discovered in week three.

cta.title: Ask about a course
cta.body: Tell us what you want to learn and where you are starting from, and we will say whether we have something that fits.

about.title: About SofinWave Academy

about.lede: SofinWave Academy is the teaching arm of SofinWave, a software consulting team based in Vietnam. Most of the engineering material began as the documents we wrote to train our own new hires, which is also why it is unusually concrete.

sections.heading: Practitioners, not career instructors
sections.body: Everyone who teaches here works in the field they teach. That has a cost — we run fewer cohorts than a dedicated school would — and a benefit, which is that the examples are current and the answers to "does this happen in real projects" are first-hand.

sections.heading: What we do not claim
sections.body: We are not an accredited institution and do not issue recognised qualifications. What you get is the material, the practice, and access to people who do the work. If you need formal accreditation, we are not it, and we would rather say so now.
